client: I've been really struggling this past week with this big presentation I have coming up at our annual conference. Yesterday during practice I completely blanked — just forgot everything I was supposed to say — and now I can't stop replaying that moment in my head. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because the presentation is next week and I don't see how therapy fixes the fact that I just... froze.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds really heavy — the anxiety in your voice tells me this moment is weighing on you more than your words alone convey, and that makes complete sense given how much this presentation means to you. That moment of blanking has turned into a story your mind keeps replaying, one that's whispering "this is proof I'll fail" — but one difficult practice run is evidence of anxiety, not of your actual capability. I hear your skepticism about whether talking helps, and I want to work *with* that — let's focus on something concrete: what we can do right now to interrupt that replay loop and rebuild your confidence before next week.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I appreciate that you're trying to help, but I'm not sure "interrupting the replay loop" is something I can just do on command. Like, I've tried telling myself to stop thinking about it and it just makes me think about it more. What does that even look like in practice, because right now it sounds a little too simple for how stuck I actually feel?
therapist: You're absolutely right to push back on that — and the way you're speaking right now, quick and tense, tells me you're not looking for a simple fix because this doesn't *feel* simple, and I shouldn't have framed it that way. You've already discovered something really important on your own: trying to force thoughts away actually backfires, which is exactly what research on thought suppression shows — the brain treats "don't think about X" as a reason to keep checking for X. So instead of fighting the replay, we'd work on changing your *relationship* to it — noticing it without letting it be the final verdict on what will happen next week.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and the part about the brain checking for the thing you're trying not to think about... that actually does make sense to me, weirdly. Like, the more I tell myself to stop replaying that moment at work where I completely froze during the presentation, the more it just keeps coming back. But I'm not sure what "changing my relationship to it" even looks like in practice, because right now it just feels like the replay is proof that I'm going to freeze again next week.
therapist: That click of recognition you just had — "oh, *that's* why it keeps coming back" — is actually really meaningful, even if it doesn't feel like much yet, and I notice your voice has softened a little, like part of you is starting to think rather than just brace. The replay feeling like *proof* is the key thing to gently challenge here: one frozen moment is data about how anxiety affects you under pressure, not a reliable prediction of next week — your brain is pattern-matching on fear, not on your actual history of preparation and competence. "Changing your relationship to it" in practice might look like this: when the replay comes, instead of fighting it, you say to yourself *"there's that moment again — it was hard, and it doesn't tell me what happens next"* — just enough distance to stop it from being a verdict.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it works that way. But when I'm actually in the middle of that replay, it feels so real and immediate that I'm not sure I'd even remember to say that phrase to myself, let alone believe it. It's like my brain just goes straight into that loop before I can catch it.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, pitched high — tells me even *talking* about the loop pulls you right back into it, which actually proves your point: this thing has a real grip, and I don't want to minimize that. You're describing something really common but genuinely hard, which is that the tools we learn in calm moments can feel completely out of reach once the anxiety takes over — so rather than relying on remembering a phrase *during* the spiral, we'd practice it enough *now*, while you're here and grounded, that it starts to become more automatic. Would you be willing to try it together right now, just so your brain has at least one experience of it working before next week?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... yeah, okay, we can try it. But I want to be honest — part of me feels kind of silly doing this stuff in here, like it's going to feel forced and fake and then I'll just feel worse when it doesn't work in the moment. I don't know, maybe I'm just being resistant, but that's genuinely what I'm worried about.
therapist: The fact that you're naming that fear out loud — that it'll feel silly, forced, and then fail you — actually tells me you're not being resistant, you're being honest, and that's exactly what good therapy needs. Your voice sounds a little stretched right now, like you're bracing for disappointment before we've even started, which makes sense given how much is riding on next week. But here's something worth holding onto: feeling forced and fake at first is *normal* with any new skill — it doesn't mean it's not working, it means your brain hasn't practiced it enough yet to make it feel natural.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that — that the awkwardness is just part of the process. But I keep thinking about the presentation specifically, like, what if I freeze up in the middle of it and the breathing thing just makes me more aware of how panicked I am instead of calming me down? It's not just abstract worry, it's that I've tried to "just breathe" before and it didn't do anything except make me feel like I was failing at breathing on top of everything else.
therapist: "Failing at breathing on top of everything else" — that phrase says so much, and I want you to know that experience is real and common, not a sign that you're broken or doing it wrong. Your voice is moving fast and pitched high even now, which tells me this specific fear — of the tool making things worse — isn't abstract for you, it's visceral and earned from actual experience. So let's set aside generic breathing advice entirely, because what you actually need isn't a calming trick but a way to stay *functional* when panic hits — which looks less like "breathe and relax" and more like having a concrete anchor, like a specific line you've rehearsed so many times it comes out even when your mind goes blank.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, when you put it that way — a rehearsed line instead of trying to calm down — that actually sounds less impossible than what I've been attempting. But I'm already second-guessing it, because what if even that line just disappears when I'm in the middle of it, like everything else does? I guess what scares me most is that I've tried to prepare before and it always feels like the panic just... erases whatever I thought I had ready.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — soft but fast, like you're holding something fragile — tells me this fear of panic "erasing" your preparation isn't just worry, it's something you've lived through enough times that it feels like a certainty. But here's what's worth examining: panic hasn't actually erased *everything* every time — you've gotten through hard moments before, even imperfectly, which means your brain is overgeneralizing one outcome into an absolute rule. The goal with a rehearsed anchor isn't to outsmart panic, it's to build something so deeply grooved that it survives it — and that only happens through repetition, which is exactly what we can start doing right now if you're willing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard not to feel like you're being a little optimistic about how bad it actually gets. When panic hits before a presentation, it's not like I just stumble a little — my mind genuinely goes blank, like someone pulled a plug, and I walk out feeling like I failed even when people tell me it went fine. I guess I can try the repetition thing, but I'm honestly not sure how practicing something in a calm room is going to help when the real moment feels completely different.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but fast, pitched high — tells me you're not pushing back to be difficult, you're trying to make sure I actually understand how severe this gets, and I want you to know I hear that: this isn't mild nerves, it's a full shutdown, and you've learned not to trust your own sense of how it went because the inside experience and the outside reality feel completely disconnected. That gap — where people say "it went fine" and you still feel like you failed — is actually one of the most important things we've touched on today, because it suggests your internal alarm system is misfiring rather than accurately reporting what's happening. And you're right that a calm room isn't the same as a conference stage, but the research on this is clear: repetition in calm conditions *does* transfer, not because it eliminates panic, but because it builds a pathway deep enough that some of it survives even a full shutdown.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying about the alarm system misfiring, and part of me wants to believe that, but it's hard when the evidence feels so real in the moment. Like, my hands were literally shaking during the last presentation, and I stumbled over my words twice, so it's not like I'm imagining the whole thing. I guess what scares me about the repetition idea is that I've practiced before and it didn't stop the shutdown from happening, so what makes this time different?
therapist: Your voice is stretched tight right now, fast and high, like you're bracing for me to dismiss what your body actually went through — and I won't, because shaking hands and stumbled words are real, and you deserve to have that acknowledged rather than explained away. But here's the honest CBT reframe: those things happened *and* you kept going, which means the shutdown wasn't total, even when it felt like it was — your brain is filing this under "proof of failure" when it could just as accurately be filed under "I got through something really hard." What makes repetition different this time isn't the repetition itself — it's that we're pairing it with changing what your brain does with that evidence, so the shaking becomes "my body is activated" rather than "I'm failing."
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that framing, I really do. But my brain keeps coming back to the fact that everyone in that room saw me fall apart, and no amount of reframing changes what they witnessed. It's like you're asking me to update my own story, but I can't control the story they're all telling about me right now.
therapist: Your voice is carrying something heavier than your words alone — high, fast, tight — like this fear of what others think isn't just a worry, it's a weight you've been holding since that moment, and that makes complete sense. But I want to gently hold up a mirror to something: you said everyone saw you "fall apart," and I want to ask — is that what actually happened, or is that the story *your* alarm system wrote about what they saw, given that the same alarm system told you previous presentations failed when people said they went fine? You can't control their story, that's true — but right now the person being hardest on you, the one whose story matters most to how you feel walking into that room next week, is you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
